power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.487", "p=0.487"), Sentence = c("Median [IQR] ASO levels were 400 IU [400-800] in the control group (n=14) and 400 IU in the intervention group (n=18), with no statistically significant difference (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.487).", "Median [IQR] ASO levels were 400 IU [400-800] in the control group (n=14) and 400 IU [200-700] in the intervention group (n=18), with no statistically significant difference (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.487)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, yet no therapy targets its underlying autoimmune mechanisms.[ 1],[2] We combined transcriptomic analyses of rheumatic mitral valves tissues with a translational approach.
Using a panel of 750 mRNAs, we found a marked upregulation of B-cell-related pathways, including CD20-associated and multiple immunoglobulin genes, supporting a pathogenic role of B cells in RHD.
We therefore evaluated an anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody (Rituximab), in a feasibility study in children with RHD, in Dakar, Sénégal.

Treatment was well tolerated, and in the following RCT first year preliminary safety analysis asked by the ethical committee, children who received rituximab showed a decrease in anti-streptolysin O titers and clinical improvement compared to controls.
This proof-of-concept reveals B cells as a therapeutic target and suggests that an anti-CD20 agent may represent a potential disease-modifying therapy for RHD.

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a major global public health problem, affecting more than 40 million people worldwide and causing 300,000 to 400,000 deaths each year. [1] The burden of disease is disproportionately high in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and parts of Oceania. [2] Although age-standardized mortality rates from RHD have declined since 1990, the absolute number of cases and deaths has remained high due to population growth. [3] Consequently, RHD is expected to persist as a leading cause of preventable cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, particularly among children, adolescents, and young adults in lowresource settings. [4] RHD is an autoimmune condition triggered by untreated Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis.

text.text: Current management strategies are first directed against the bacterial infection.

Primary prevention relies on oral penicillin to treat streptococcal infections, while secondary prevention consists of intramuscular benzathine penicillin administered every three weeks, often until the age of 21 years. [3] Although this prevention has proven to be effective in randomized control trials (RCT), its implementation is limited in practice due to the complications and potential risks associated with repeated intramuscular injections, including anaphylactic shock and death, leading to the suppression of its use in many countries. [12] Treatment of ARF episodes and heart failure is largely symptomatic, with valve replacement surgery available only to a minority of patients because of the limited availability of cardiac surgical infrastructure in endemic regions.

text.text: Importantly, no specific therapy currently targets the underlying immuneinflammatory mechanisms of RHD, representing a major therapeutic gap.
To address this issue, we investigated RHD immunopathophysiology.
We explored gene expression patterns in diseased mitral valves using advanced immunologic tools, to identify key molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in RHD.

Based on these findings, we evaluated the rationale for targeting CD20-positive B-cells and report the interim safety analysis of the first year (as required by the ethical committee) of an ongoing RCT assessing the potential therapeutic role of an anti-CD20 agent (rituximab) in children with RHD. text.text: Differentially expressed genes were predominantly enriched in immune pathways involving B and T lymphocytes, natural killer (NK) cells, monocytes/macrophages, and pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling.
Among these immune signatures, B-cell-associated transcripts showed particularly strong and consistent upregulation in rheumatic valves.

Differential expression analysis demonstrated marked enrichment of several B-cell markers, including MS4A1 (CD20), CD19, CD22, MS4A2, together with numerous immunoglobulin genes, such as IGHG1, IGHG2, IGHG3, IGHG4, IGHM, IGHA1, IGKC, and IGLC1, which ranked among the most significantly upregulated transcripts (Figure 2).

Gene-level analyses further confirmed significantly increased expression of MS4A1, MS4A2, CD22, and CD19 in rheumatic compared with control valves (Figure 3).

text.text: Similarly, immunoglobulin-related transcripts, including IGHM, IGHA1, IGKC, and IGLC1, were markedly increased in RHD samples.
Together, these findings are consistent with enhanced Bcell infiltration and/or activation, accompanied by a prominent antibody-producing cell signature within diseased valve tissue.
In agreement with the transcriptomic data, histological analysis demonstrated the presence of CD20-positive B-cells within the inflammatory infiltrate of rheumatic valves (Figure 4).

text.text: The concordance between transcriptional and histological findings provides complementary . evidence for prominent B-cell involvement in the chronic inflammatory response associated with RHD valve pathology.
Genes associated with CD4+ helper T cells, CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells were also significantly upregulated, including CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD4, ZAP70, GNLY, GZMA, and KLRK1.
The increased expression of chemokine receptors such as CXCR3 suggests active recruitment and retention of these cells within inflamed valve tissue.
In addition, a monocyte/macrophage signature was observed, characterized by elevated expression of CCR2, CX3CR1, FCGR1A, FCGR2A, FCGR3A, ITGAM, ITGAX, TREM1, LST1, and S100A9.
This profile is consistent with chronic innate immune activation and sustained tissue inflammation.
Key inflammatory mediators were significantly overexpressed in rheumatic valves, notably TNF, alongside enrichment of IL-6-related signalling pathways.
These findings indicate ongoing inflammatory signalling that may contribute to progressive valvular damage and fibrosis.

Taken together, transcriptomic and expression distribution analyses reveal that rheumatic mitral valves are characterized by a complex immune infiltrate involving B-cells, T/NK lymphocytes, and monocyte/macrophage populations.

Based on the particularly strong and reproducible overexpression of CD20-related and immunoglobulin genes, confirmed at both differential expression and distribution levels, we hypothesized that B lymphocytes play a major role in RHD pathophysiology and that B cell depletion using anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (Rituximab) would be protective.
Notably, no suitable animal model currently exists for RHD, further justifying the need for carefully monitored clinical evaluation.
Having identified CD20-positive B-cells as a plausible therapeutic target, the next step was to evaluate the feasibility and safety of pharmacological B-cell depletion in children with RHD.

Rituximab was selected as the anti-CD20 agent because it is a widely available, affordable generic drug in many countries and is well tolerated by paediatric patients. [14] Given the potential risk of impairing humoral immunity in children living in low-resource settings, with inherent increased risk for multiple viral, bacteria and parasite potential infections, we adopted a cautious stepwise approach after approval from the ethical committee.

text.text: Since January 2023, fifteen paediatric patients with severe RHD received rituximab in addition to the classical treatment, as part of a feasibility study in the paediatric ward Albert Royer of the Fann University Hospital in Dakar, Senegal.

Patients in the intervention group received two infusions, one at baseline (day 0) and a second 14 days later at a dose of 375 mg/m² administered intravenously, to obtain a full and prolonged B cell depletion. [16] Patients were followed for six months, with particular attention to infusion-related reactions, infections and cardiac adverse events.

text.text: Two transient complications were observed: vomiting occurred in two patients who had eaten immediately prior to the infusion.
After implementing a recommendation that patients should fast before treatment, no further cases were reported.
No severe infusion reactions, infectious complications, or delayed adverse events were observed during the six-month follow-up period.
Overall, rituximab administration was considered feasible and well tolerated in this preliminary safety cohort.
Consequently, and based on this favourable safety profile, it was decided to assess the efficacy of rituximab in a RCT.

Ethical approval was granted for a RCT (Pan African Clinical Trials registry PACTR202504487625242), contingent upon a planned interim safety analysis after the first year of the study focused on potential side effects (supplementary files).
Two medical doctors (HI, MKS) assessed independently the results.
In case of disagreement, the decision was made by a third person blinded for the treatment (EM).

Thirtyseven participants (17 in the standard treatment group and 20 in the intervention group), enrolled during the first year, have completed their follow-up and were included in this interim safety analysis.
All patients received the standard treatment consisting of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin or erythromycin in cases of severe penicillin allergy.
Patients in the intervention group received two infusions of rituximab, one at baseline and a second dose 14 days later.
Total Anti-Streptolysin O (ASO) antibody titers, irrespective of immunoglobulin isotype, were measured at baseline before the first infusion, and again 6 months after treatment initiation.
ASO antibodies reflect a prior immune response to Streptococcus pyogenes, even in the absence of active infection.
In the control group (n=17), the median [IQR] age was 14.0 years [12.0-15.0], with 5 females (29%) and 12 males (71%).
In the intervention group (n=20), the median [IQR] age was 11.5 years [10.0-14.2], with 12 females (60%) and 8 males (40%).
Two transient complications were observed after anti-CD20 agent infusion.
One patient experienced faintness approximately six hours after infusion, associated with a sensation of palpitations.
Electrocardiographic (ECG) monitoring did not reveal any abnormal findings.
A second patient reported palpitations during the infusion; ECG recording showed a supraventricular arrhythmia, which resolved without further complications.
During the 6 months follow-up, two patients required cardiac surgery, one in the intervention group and one in the control group.
No death occurred during this 6month period.
To illustrate the results of the auto immune molecular mechanisms, the clinical and biological results of the first year of the study are given.
Among the 32 patients with available ASO measurements, baseline titers were similar between groups.
Median [IQR] ASO levels were 400 IU [400-800] in the control group (n=14) and 400 IU  in the intervention group (n=18), with no statistically significant difference (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.487).

Six months after inclusion, the median ASO titers were 300 IU  in the control group and 100 IU  in the intervention group, showing a significant difference between groups (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.017).
A decrease in ASO titers of at least 50% was observed in 12 of 18 patients (66.7%) treated with anti-CD20 agent, compared with 5 of 14 patients (35.7%) in the control group.

Our proof of concept provides convergent molecular, histological, biological and clinical evidence supporting a central pathogenic role for B lymphocytes in the pathophysiology of RHD.
We show that CD20-positive B cells infiltrate rheumatic valvular lesions and that Bcell depletion with rituximab is feasible and appears relatively safe in children with severe RHD.
Together, these findings identify B cells as a potential therapeutic target in a disease for which no disease-modifying treatment currently exists.
RHD remains one of the most neglected cardiovascular diseases worldwide.

Although it has virtually disappeared from most high-income countries owing to improved living conditions, widespread antibiotic use and structured prevention programs, it continues to cause substantial morbidity and mortality in low-and middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. [2], [3] Systematic echocardiographic screening performed 20 years ago by our group and others demonstrated that the burden of childhood RHD was approximately ten-fold higher than previously estimated using World Health Organization case definitions, leading to a reassessment of the global burden of disease. [17] These observations contributed to the revision of the Jones diagnostic criteria in 2015 and to the World Health Organization's recognition of RHD as a global health priority in 2018. [18], [19] Despite this renewed attention, treatment strategies remain largely unchanged without any therapeutic innovation.

text.text: NanoString profiling enabled the simultaneous analysis of approximately 750 immune-related genes, providing, to our knowledge, the most comprehensive molecular characterization of rheumatic valvular tissue reported to date.
These observations suggest that B cells may play a more sustained role in disease propagation than previously appreciated.
Beyond antibody production, they may contribute to chronic valvular inflammation through antigen presentation and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6.
This interpretation is consistent with observations in other clinical settings, where rituximab-induced B-cell depletion may precede changes in circulating antibody levels.

In cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, clinical improvement may occur before reductions in cryoglobulin or rheumatoid factor levels, while in acute myocardial infarction, rituximab induced rapid B-cell depletion without measurable changes in circulating immunoglobulin levels. [31], [32] Consistent with this mechanism, rituximab treatment resulted in a marked depletion of circulating B cells together with a significant reduction in ASO titres.

Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells through complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and apoptosis while largely preserving T-cell immunity. [33] This selective immunomodulation probably explains the favourable short-term safety profile observed in our cohort despite the high background burden of infectious diseases. [14], [15] Nevertheless, longer follow-up remains essential, particularly to assess immune reconstitution and the potential risk of hepatitis virus reactivation.

text.text: Clinical observations should be interpreted cautiously because this proof-of-concept study was not designed to evaluate efficacy.
The clinical and biological data presented here primarily serve to support the mechanistic findings.
Nevertheless, the rapid improvement observed was accompanied by meaningful functional recovery, including return to school, work or resumption of physical activity.
In paediatric populations, these outcomes constitute important indicators of quality of life that may better reflect disease burden than conventional clinical endpoints alone.
School attendance is particularly relevant, as prolonged absence may have lasting educational and developmental consequences.
Although preliminary, these findings raise the possibility that B-cell depletion may represent the first disease-modifying therapeutic strategy for RHD.

Rituximab has an established role in several autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and has increasingly become available in resource-limited settings. [34], [35], [36], [37], [38] Its application to RHD has not previously been explored, reflecting the considerable logistical and infrastructural challenges of conducting interventional studies in endemic regions, together with competing public health priorities.

text.text: In contrast, other targeted immunomodulatory strategies remain largely unexplored, and no alternative biological therapy has demonstrated efficacy in RHD.

Preventive vaccination against S. pyogenes represents another promising avenue, with several M-protein and non-M-protein vaccine candidates currently under development; however, no vaccine is yet available for clinical practice. text.text: First, the clinicians' awareness of treatment allocation tempers conclusions regarding clinical efficacy and leaves open the possibility of observer and expectation bias.

Second, the limited sample size and relatively short follow-up do not allow robust assessment of long-term efficacy, durability of B-cell depletion, immune reconstitution or progression of valvular disease.

Third, follow-up in resource-limited settings remains challenging because of socioeconomic constraints, transportation barriers and restricted access to healthcare, resulting in incomplete follow-up for some participants and missing data.
In addition, laboratory and imaging resources were necessarily constrained, potentially affecting data completeness and standardization.

Finally, as healthcare systems and disease epidemiology vary substantially across sub-Saharan Africa, external validation in other endemic settings will be required before these findings can be generalized.
However, these constraints should not be viewed solely as methodological limitations but also as an inherent feature of pragmatic clinical research in endemic settings.
If therapeutic innovation for RHD is to benefit the populations most affected by the disease, evidence must be generated under the conditions in which care is actually delivered.
Advancing clinical research in low-and middleincome countries therefore requires acknowledging these challenges while investing in the infrastructure needed to progressively overcome them.
An important clinical question is whether B-cell depletion should ultimately be considered earlier in the course of RHD, before irreversible structural valve damage has developed.
The current study included only children with advanced valvular disease, and whether earlier intervention could modify the natural history of RHD remains unknown.
Of note, three deaths occurred after the first year and were therefore not included in this interim analysis.
All deaths were of cardiovascular origin, reflecting the severity of the patients' underlying condition.
Two occurred in the control group and one in the Rituximab group.
The ongoing RCT, powered to enrol 108 participants per group, will determine whether rituximab confers durable disease modification rather than transient suppression of inflammation.

Echocardiographic assessment of structural valve progression, the key endpoint for establishing disease modification, will require substantially longer follow-up, with definitive data expected in approximately three years.
The integration of clinical, biological and echocardiographic outcomes will therefore be essential to establish whether B-cell depletion truly alters disease progression.
This trial also raises an important ethical question.
Given the early clinical improvement observed, should treatment continue to be withheld from children randomized to the control group while awaiting structural echocardiographic endpoints?
These children remain at risk of prolonged disability, school interruption and progressive cardiac damage.

After careful consideration, the Data and Safety Monitoring Board and the ethics committee concluded that continuation of the RCT remained ethically justified because definitive evidence of disease modification has not yet been established.

In conclusion, the concordance between molecular profiling, tissue pathology, biological response and early clinical improvement supports a previously underappreciated role for B cells in RHD pathogenesis.

Although causality and long-term disease modification remain to be demonstrated, these findings introduce a mechanistically informed therapeutic strategy for a disease that has seen little innovation for decades.
Confirmation in adequately powered randomized trials and in independent endemic populations will determine whether B-celltargeted therapy can redefine the treatment paradigm for RHD.
Mitral valve tissue samples were obtained from 32 patients with severe RHD undergoing surgical valve replacement.
Control valve samples were obtained from 9 nonrheumatic valves that included non-immune valvulopathies.
All samples were collected at the time of surgery and processed according to local ethical and regulatory approvals.
Gene expression profiling was performed using a nCounter platform (Bruker spatial biology) targeting a predefined panel of 750 mRNAs.

This panel was designed to explore inflammatory pathways, immune cell populations, and humoral immune responses, with a particular focus on mechanisms suspected to be involved in autoimmune processes.
Raw counts were normalized following the manufacturer's recommendations.

Differential gene expression analysis was conducted to identify significantly dysregulated genes between rheumatic and control valves, using a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change of 1.
To support transcriptomic findings, histochemical and histological analyses were performed on valve tissue sections to localize immune cell populations.

Based on the identification of a strong B-cell signature in rheumatic mitral valves, a study was conducted to assess the safety of anti-CD20 therapy in children with RHD in the paediatric ward Albert Royer of the Fann University Hospital in Dakar, Sénégal.
Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody of the IgG1 subtype directed against the CD20 antigen, a surface molecule expressed on pre-B and mature B lymphocytes.
Binding of rituximab to CD20 leads to B-cell depletion through multiple mechanisms, including complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and induction of apoptosis.
Rituximab does not target plasma cells, allowing pre-existing immunoglobulin production to be partially preserved.
It is widely used in hematologic malignancies and autoimmune diseases and has a well-characterized safety profile across diverse clinical settings.
Fifteen children with confirmed RHD received rituximab at a dose of 375 mg/m² administered intravenously at baseline (day 0) and a second identical dose 14 days later.
Given the potential risks associated with B-cell depletion in children living in settings with high infectious burden, this phase of the study was specifically designed to prioritize safety.
Patients were followed for a period of six months after infusion.
Clinical evaluations, biological assessments, and ECG monitoring were performed during scheduled follow-up visits.
All adverse events were systematically recorded.
An adverse event was defined as any harmful medical occurrence observed in a participant during the research period, whether or not it was considered related to the investigational product.
An adverse effect was defined as any harmful and unintended reaction suspected to be related to the research procedures or to rituximab administration.

The attribution of an adverse event as an adverse effect was determined jointly by the investigator and the study sponsor, based on the clinical description, temporal relationship to treatment administration, potential alternative aetiologies, and clinical evolution.

Adverse events were classified as serious if they resulted in death, were life-threatening, required hospitalization or prolongation of hospitalization, caused significant or persistent disability, or resulted in congenital anomaly.
Medically important events not meeting these criteria but requiring specific monitoring were also considered serious.
Any pregnancy occurring during the study period and any new safety signal potentially modifying the benefitrisk balance were recorded as serious safety events.
The primary objective of this pilot phase was the identification of safety signals associated with rituximab.
No efficacy outcomes were evaluated during this phase.
Then, we proceeded to formally evaluate the potential efficacy of rituximab in an open RCT.
Ethical approval was granted, with the requirement to present interim safety analysis after one year focused on potential clinical and biological side effects (Supplementary files).
The objective of this analysis was to confirm the safety profile of rituximab during the study.
The primary endpoint (echocardiographic rheumatic valvular lesions) was not assessed as part of this interim safety analysis.
Therefore, this analysis has no impact on the statistical power, sample size calculation, or planned primary efficacy analysis, all of which will remain unchanged.
The trial is conducted in Senegal at a single tertiary paediatric centre specializing in the management of ARF and RHD.
Children aged between 5 and 17 years with confirmed ARF and at least one severe active rheumatic valvular lesion documented by echocardiography were enrolled.
Written informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians prior to inclusion.
Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either the intervention group or the control group.
Randomization was performed to ensure equal allocation between groups.
The absence of blinding was mitigated by the use of objective outcome measures, standardized follow-up procedures, and identical clinical monitoring in both groups.
Inclusion criteria were: confirmed diagnosis of ARF with rheumatic valvular involvement, age between 5 and 17 years, and signed informed consent.

Exclusion criteria included active or chronic infections (HIV, hepatitis B or C, tuberculosis, Epstein-Barr virus), history of severe or recurrent infections, immunodeficiency or autoimmune disease, malignancy, diabetes, recent use of immunosuppressive therapies, prior exposure to monoclonal antibodies, hypersensitivity to rituximab, penicillin, acetylsalicylic acid or paracetamol, recent or planned vaccination, pre-existing heart failure, renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance <45 mL/min/1.73 m²), pregnancy, Guillain-Barré syndrome, abnormal baseline laboratory values (severe cytopenias or elevated liver enzymes), or participation in another interventional trial within the previous six months.

text.text: Patients were recruited among children with ARF regularly followed at the paediatric ward Albert Royer of the Fann University Hospital in Dakar, Sénégal.

All participants received standard-of-care therapy consisting of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (1-2 million IU/day in two divided doses for 10 days), or erythromycin in cases of severe penicillin allergy, and acetylsalicylic acid at a dose of 75 mg/kg/day for four weeks.
Patients randomized to the intervention group additionally received rituximab at a dose of 375 mg/m² administered intravenously at baseline (day 0) and a second identical dose 14 days later.

Patients in the control group did not receive rituximab but continued standard therapy and additionally received a 5% glucose solution (Glucidion G5) as a placebo, administered intravenously at baseline (day 0) and again 14 days later.
Patients were evaluated at baseline, day 14, and at 3 and 6 months after treatment initiation.
Each visit included a clinical examination, blood sampling, ECG, and transthoracic echocardiography.
Biological improvement was defined as a decrease of at least 50% in ASO antibody titers measured 6 months after treatment initiation.
ASO titers reflect a prior humoral immune response to Streptococcus pyogenes infection, independent of active bacterial presence.

Clinical improvement was defined as either a return to school, work, or previous physical activities, or a transition from arthralgia at inclusion to absence of arthralgia at 6 months, provided that physical activity remained stable and did not deteriorate.
Patients were considered stable or worsened if neither of these criteria was met.

The analysis reveals a marked enrichment of significantly upregulated B-cell-associated genes in RHD valves.
Notably, immunoglobulin genes (IGHG1, IGHG2, IGHG3, IGHG4, IGHA1, IGKC, IGLC1), display both high statistical significance and large effect sizes.
These genes are among the most strongly upregulated transcripts in rheumatic valves, indicating increased Bcell presence and/or activation within diseased tissue.

In parallel, genes related to T lymphocytes and natural killer cells (CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD4, ZAP70, KLRK1, GNLY) and to monocyte/macrophage populations (CCR2, CX3CR1, FCGR1A, FCGR2A, FCGR3A, ITGAM, ITGAX, TREM1, LST1, S100A9) are also significantly upregulated, reflecting a broader inflammatory infiltrate.

Importantly, the clustering of CD20-related and immunoglobulin genes in the upper quadrant of the plot indicates that B-cell-associated pathways represent one of the most prominent and statistically robust differences between RHD and control valves.
This finding provides a strong molecular rationale for targeting CD20-positive B-cells in rheumatic heart disease.

Genes encoding canonical B-cell surface markers, including MS4A1 (CD20), MS4A2, and CD22, show significantly higher expression in RHD valves compared with controls.
In parallel, multiple immunoglobulin-related genes (IGLC1, IGHA1, IGHM, IGKC) are also markedly upregulated in rheumatic samples, reflecting enhanced local antibody-related activity.

The consistent increase across both B-cell identity markers and immunoglobulin genes indicates not only an increased presence of B lymphocytes within rheumatic valve tissue, but also their functional activation.
The magnitude and reproducibility of these differences support the conclusion that B-cell-driven immune mechanisms represent a key molecular feature distinguishing rheumatic from control valves.
